newsitem.title: CHINA: China calls in clerics in restive Moslem region.
newsitem.headline: China calls in clerics in restive Moslem region.

text.p: China's communist rulers have called on Moslem clerics to help ensure stability in the restive northwestern region of Xinjiang after seizing 11 tonnes of explosives in an anti-crime crackdown.

Keyum Bawudun, the Communist Party's deputy secretary in Xinjiang, urged about 300 Moslem clerics recently to make contributions to the stability of the region that has been rocked repeatedly by anti-Chinese unrest in recent months, the Xinjiang Daily said in an edition seen in Beijing on Monday.
"It is the unshirkable responsibility of clerics," Keyum Bawudun was quoted as saying in the June 11 edition of the newspaper.
"We must trust, rely on, protect and support clerics," Keyum Bawudun said.
"A majority of clerics are good, patriotic and for maintaining stability," he said, hinting that some religious leaders may sympathise with the independence movement.

He warned against religious fanaticism. "We will resolutely and severely deal a blow to those who engage in illegal activities under the cloak of religion and the small group of people who develop religion extremist forces," he said.
Xinjiang has no single high-profile religious leader, unlike the Himalayan region of Tibet, where monks and nuns view the exiled Dalai Lama as their god-king.

The call for clerics to help to restore stability in the region came after Chinese authorities seized 11,000 kg (24,000 lb) of explosives and uncovered 83 hideouts illegally selling firearms between March and May as part of a government crackdown on crime.
The authorities also seized 110,000 detonators, 638 illegal firearms and 10,000 rounds of ammunition, the newspaper said.
Xinjiang has been rocked by a string of bombings and riotings since February.
In May, Chinese authorities executed eight people in the regional capital Urumqi for bombings, murders and robberies that left nine people dead.
The group planted home-made bombs on public buses that blew up within minutes of each other in Urumqi on February 25, killing nine people and injuring 58 others.
The attacks coincided with funeral rites in Beijing for paramount leader Deng Xiaoping who died in February aged 92. The group planted two other bombs which did not explode.
Exiled separatists of the ethnic Uighur minority have claimed responsibility for the assaults and vowed to stage more until they gain freedom for their homeland.
Turkish-speaking Uighur militants want to set up an independent East Turkestan in Xinjiang.
In April, a self-taught expert on the Koran was executed for bombing a military jeep last year.
Riots in the western Xinjiang town of Yining last February, which began as demonstrations for Xinjiang independence and turned violent, left nine people dead and 198 injured.
Chinese authorities executed three rioters and police killed two others when they opened fire on a mob trying to rescue the death-row convicts.

Xinjiang was shaken last year by bombings and assassination attempts on officials and Moslem leaders seen as favouring Beijing, prompting authorities to intensify a crackdown on separatists as well as on underground religious activity.
Xinjiang borders Afghanistan, Pakistan and three mostly Moslem Central Asian states.
